sources.citation: Carr, Therese L. 2000. Wunambal: a language of the North-West Kimberley region, Western Australia. MA(Hons) thesis, University of New England. hdl 1959.11/16787.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: p. 2: 'Linguistically Gamberre may be regarded as a dialect of Wunambal.' Section 2.4 Stress (pp. 61-63) describes WUNAMBAL only: two- and most three-syllable words stressed on the first syllable; words of more than three syllables have primary stress on the penult and secondary on the first syllable. No Gamberre data in the stress section.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur & H. H. J. Coate. 1984. Comparative studies in Northern Kimberley languages. Pacific Linguistics C-69. Canberra: ANU. xv+262 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ch. 1 'Preliminary: phonological principles' (pp. 7-17) covers phonemes, syllable, root/word structure and morphophonemic rules but has no stress/accent section. Gambere data (from Lucich) appear only for retroflex minimal pairs (pp. 8-9) and in morphology. Stress is mentioned only incidentally for Worora, Ngarinjin and Wunambal (e.g. auxiliary *bu/*wu alternations 'affected by rules of stress', p. 251-252); nothing on where Gambere stress falls.

sources.citation: Capell, A. 1941. Notes on the Wunambal language. Oceania 11(3):295-308 (same issue: Hernandez, T. 1941. Social organization of the Drysdale River tribes, Oceania 11(3)).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Morphological notes on (southern) Wunambal; Gambre named only as the variety into which Wunambal 'merges' northwards along Admiralty Gulf. No stress or accent remarks.

sources.citation: Capell, A. 1940. The classification of languages in North and North-West Australia. Oceania 10(3):241-272; 10(4):404-433.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: General phonetic introduction for the whole N/NW Australian survey area, p. 243: 'Accent is also important, though it is difficult to set down rules for it.' Gambre appears only in the classification (grouped with the Drysdale dialects, p. 262) and comparative wordlist; no language-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. & Alan Rumsey. 2009. Worrorran revisited: the case for genetic relations among languages of the Northern Kimberley region of Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics 600. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Table 2 (p. 4): main source of data on Gambera = Capell and Coate (1984). Ch. 4 on sound correspondences has no stress discussion; the only prosodic remark is a passing reference to 'initial stressed syllables' in Unggumi (p. 22). Nothing on Gambera stress.
